posts.caption: The farrier said he'd be here between 8 and 10, which in farrier means sometime before the sun goes down. I had her brushed, picked out, and standing in the aisle by 7:45. By 11 she'd eaten her hay, untied herself twice, and knocked the fly spray off the shelf. When his truck finally pulled in at 12:20, she took one look at him and planted all four feet like she was paying rent on that spot. He asked if she'd been difficult lately. I told him she'd been perfect all morning. Then he showed up.
posts.first: My old gelding used to hear the farrier's truck before I did. He'd walk to the far corner of the pasture and stand with his back to the gate. Not running, not hiding. Just making it clear he had other plans. I'd go get him anyway, and he'd sigh the whole way in.

posts.caption: I bought him the spring I turned twenty-nine, a five-year-old gray with more opinions than training. My friends said I was too old to start over with a young horse. That was twenty-four years ago. Since then I've changed jobs twice, moved once, and gone through more barn boots than I can count. He's been in the paddock out back for all of it. These days I bring his carrot down at 6:30 with my coffee, and we both take the slope a little slower than we used to. He still nickers when the porch door opens. I still answer.
posts.first: The first year I had him, he dumped me in the arena so many times the barn owner started calling it my landing strip. I'd get up, brush off, and climb back on. Now he stands like a statue at the mounting block and waits while I get my knee situated. We worked it out.

posts.theme: the horse budget vs. the spouse
posts.quote: My husband found the feed store receipt. I told him it was a donation to a 1,200-pound charity that lives in our backyard.
posts.first: For the record, I've started paying for hay in cash. Not because I'm hiding anything. Cash is just simpler, and the hay guy appreciates it, and nobody at home needs to see a number that long printed on paper. It's a system. It's been working since about March.

posts.caption: The feed room has a sliding latch, a bungee cord, and a second hook I installed in August specifically because of him. This morning I walked in at 6:15 and found all three undone and the lid off the sweet feed bin. He was standing in the middle of the room with grain on his nose and a single piece of straw in his forelock, looking at me like I was the one who had some explaining to do. He's 38 inches tall. I have no idea how he reaches the hook. I've decided not to find out.
posts.first: My first pony could open any gate on the property except the one that led to the road, which I've always been grateful for. He'd let himself into the hay barn, eat until he was round, then let himself back out. We only knew because of the hoofprints and the empty bale.

posts.caption: She has a grooming routine and she will tell you when you've skipped a step. Curry, hard brush, soft brush, face brush, then the detangler on her tail, in that order. Last Tuesday I was running late and went straight from the hard brush to her blanket. She turned her head, looked at the soft brush sitting in the tote, then looked at me. Didn't move a foot until I picked it up. My own hair was in a clip I found in the truck. She looked better than I did, and we both knew it.
posts.first: I once spent twenty dollars on a mane detangler that smelled like coconut and used it on her before I ever thought about my own hair. My husband said the horse smelled better than our bathroom. He wasn't wrong. I've since bought a bigger bottle and stopped pretending it's only for her.

posts.caption: The weather lady said two to four inches overnight, and by 3 in the afternoon the barn was in full lockdown. Extra hay in every stall. Heated bucket plugged in and tested twice. Blankets pulled off the rack and lined up on the stall doors like school clothes laid out the night before. She watched all of it with her chin on the door and the cat asleep on her back. When I opened the gate so she could stretch her legs one last time, she looked at the sky, looked at me, and lay down in the straw.
posts.first: We lost power for two days during a storm years ago, and I spent both nights in the barn in a sleeping bag on a pile of shavings. I told everyone it was to keep an eye on the water. Mostly it was warmer out there than the house, and the company was better.
